Pembrokeshire by Motorcycle: Wales' Finest Coastline

Pembrokeshire occupies the south-western tip of Wales and contains some of Britain's most spectacular coastal scenery. The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park is the UK's only coastal national park, and riding its roads is a revelation — dramatic cliffs, golden beaches, and a succession of pretty harbours and villages.

The Coastal Circuit

A complete loop of Pembrokeshire takes about 120 miles and can be ridden in a day, though two days allows proper exploration. Start from Tenby and head west along the south coast through Pembroke to St Ann's Head. Continue north through Marloes to St David's, then east along the north coast through Newport back to Tenby.

South Coast Highlights

The south Pembrokeshire coast features dramatic limestone cliffs and the stunning beaches of Barafundle Bay (regularly voted one of Britain's best) and Broad Haven South. The roads wind through a patchwork of farmland with frequent sea views. Pembroke Castle, birthplace of Henry VII, is an impressive stop.

St David's and the West

St David's is Britain's smallest city, with a population of barely 1,600 but a magnificent medieval cathedral. The surrounding headland is wild and beautiful — the road to St David's Head passes through exposed heathland with views to Ramsey Island. The harbour at Porthgain is a hidden gem with excellent seafood at the Sloop Inn.

Pembrokeshire is often compared to Cornwall but with fewer crowds and lower prices. The locals consider this a compliment — and a closely guarded secret.

North Coast: The Preseli Hills

The Preseli Hills in north Pembrokeshire provide an unexpected mountain experience. The B4329 crosses these moorland hills, passing prehistoric sites including the quarry that provided bluestones for Stonehenge. The views from the hilltops extend across Cardigan Bay to Snowdonia on clear days. Newport is a charming coastal town at the foot of the hills.

Practical Information

  • Best season: May to September — wildflowers on the cliffs are spectacular in June
  • Fuel: Available in Tenby, Pembroke, Haverfordwest, and St David's
  • Accommodation: Book ahead for summer — Tenby and St David's fill up fast
  • Road conditions: B-roads can be narrow with blind bends. Watch for farm vehicles
  • Access: M4 to Carmarthen, then A40 to Haverfordwest — about 4.5 hours from London

Wildlife Bonus

Pembrokeshire is one of Britain's best wildlife destinations. Puffins nest on Skomer Island (May-July), grey seals haul out on the beaches, and dolphins and porpoises are regularly spotted from the cliff-tops. faq.q: How long is the Pembrokeshire coastal loop?
faq.a: A complete loop of Pembrokeshire is about 120 miles and can be ridden in a day, though two days allows proper exploration. A good route starts from Tenby, heads west along the south coast through Pembroke to St Ann's Head, then north through Marloes to St David's and back along the north coast.

faq.q: What is special about St David's?
faq.a: St David's is Britain's smallest city, with a population of barely 1,600 but a magnificent medieval cathedral. The surrounding headland is wild and beautiful, with the road to St David's Head crossing exposed heathland to views over Ramsey Island. The nearby harbour at Porthgain has excellent seafood.

faq.q: When is the best time to ride Pembrokeshire?
faq.a: May to September is best, and the wildflowers on the cliffs are spectacular in June. Book accommodation ahead for summer, as Tenby and St David's fill up fast. B-roads can be narrow with blind bends, so watch for farm vehicles, and enjoy the wildlife from puffins to seals and dolphins.

faq.q: Is there a mountain section in Pembrokeshire?
faq.a: Yes. The Preseli Hills in the north provide an unexpected moorland experience. The B4329 crosses these hills, passing prehistoric sites including the quarry that provided the bluestones for Stonehenge. On clear days the views extend across Cardigan Bay to Snowdonia, with Newport a charming town at the foot.
